issues.subcategory: inconsistent test statistics between text and table
issues.description: The regressions-out effect is reported in the text as B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01, but Table 5 reports B = 0.25, z = 2.65 for the same measure. These values are inconsistent and cannot both be correct. The discrepancy in both the estimate (0.3 vs 0.25) and the z-value (3.12 vs 2.65) suggests either a reporting error in the text or the table reflects a different model specification. This undermines confidence in the reported results.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01). ... Regressions-out | 0.14 (0.1) | 0.17 (0.1) | 0.03 | 0.25 | z = 2.65 **

issues.subcategory: inconsistent go-past time estimates between text and table
issues.description: The go-past time congruency effect is reported in the text as B = 41, t = 3.837, but Table 5 reports B = 43, t = 3.76 for the same measure. Both the estimate and the t-value differ between the two locations. This internal inconsistency suggests copy-paste errors or that different model runs are being reported, making it impossible to determine which values are correct.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) ... Go-past time | 458 (129) | 507 (125) | 49 | 43 | t = 3.76 ***

issues.subcategory: incorrect p-value reporting for token specificity interaction
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the token-based interaction between specificity and condition is reported as 'z = 0.60, p < 0.01'. A z-value of 0.60 corresponds to a p-value of approximately 0.55, which is far from significant. A z-value of 0.60 cannot yield p < 0.01 under any standard statistical framework. This appears to be a typographical error where either the z-value or the p-value is wrong, but it is impossible to determine which without access to the raw data.
issues.quote: the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.subcategory: incorrect degrees of freedom for F-test
issues.description: The authors report an F-test as 'F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01' to test whether the regression slope differs from 1. An F-test comparing a slope to a fixed value requires two degrees of freedom (numerator and denominator), yet only one is reported. The denominator degrees of freedom (number of suffixes minus parameters) is missing, making it impossible to verify this test. Additionally, the relationship between the t-value (t = 25.32) and the F-value (F = 7.44) is inconsistent: if t = 25.32, then F = t² = 641.3, not 7.44.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: contradictory suffix counts
issues.description: The methods section states that 154 written suffixes were identified in total. After excluding suffixes occurring in fewer than 20 words (described as 64 suffixes), the text states 95 suffixes remain. However, 154 minus 64 equals 90, not 95. This arithmetic error is internally inconsistent and raises questions about the accuracy of the computational analysis reporting.
issues.quote: This process revealed 154 written suffixes in total... we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes

issues.subcategory: contradictory suffix frequency counts in Table 2 vs Appendix A
issues.description: Table 2 lists the type frequency of +ness as 1241 and +ity as 506, but Appendix A lists +ness type frequency as 1242 and +ity as 508. Similarly, Table 2 lists +ment type frequency as 251 but Appendix A lists it as 257. These discrepancies suggest different versions of the analysis were used for different parts of the paper, undermining confidence in the computational results.

issues.subcategory: contradictory diagnosticity values between Table 2 and Appendix A
issues.description: Table 2 reports type diagnosticity for +ical as 0.97, but Appendix A reports it as 0.965. Table 2 reports +ous type diagnosticity as 0.99, but Appendix A reports 0.991. Table 2 reports +less as 0.97, Appendix A as 0.975. While these are minor numerical differences, they suggest different computational runs or rounding conventions were applied inconsistently, and the discrepancies are not explained.

issues.subcategory: contradictory type frequency for +er between Table 2 and Appendix A
issues.description: Table 2 reports the type frequency of +er as 1091, while Appendix A reports it as 1198. This is a substantial discrepancy of 107 words and cannot be attributed to rounding. Similarly, Table 2 reports +ous type frequency as 225 while Appendix A reports 227. These inconsistencies suggest the analyses in different sections of the paper were not conducted on the same dataset.

issues.subcategory: missing random slope structure in mixed models
issues.description: All three experiments use mixed models with only random intercepts for subjects (and suffixes in Experiment 3), but no random slopes. The model specification 'glmer(response ~ condition + (1|subject))' does not allow the effect of condition to vary across subjects. Given that individual differences in morphological sensitivity are well-documented and theoretically relevant to the paper's claims, the absence of random slopes for the key predictor (condition/diagnosticity/specificity) risks inflated Type I error rates and overstated conclusions about the reliability of effects.
issues.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.subcategory: absence of pre-registration
issues.description: The paper reports three experiments with multiple dependent variables (especially Experiment 3 with six eye-movement measures), multiple predictors, and graded follow-up analyses, but there is no mention of pre-registration. The authors explicitly acknowledge having no concrete predictions about which eye-movement measures would be affected ('We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected'). This combination of exploratory analysis without pre-registration, multiple DVs, and post-hoc selection of significant outcomes substantially inflates the risk of false positives.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.subcategory: no correction for multiple comparisons across eye-movement measures
issues.description: Experiment 3 tests six eye-movement measures (skipping, first fixation duration, first run dwell time, go-past time, regressions-in, regressions-out) without any correction for multiple comparisons. With six tests at α = 0.05, the familywise error rate is approximately 26%. The two significant effects (go-past time and regressions-out) would not survive even a simple Bonferroni correction (required p < 0.0083). The authors do not acknowledge this limitation.
issues.quote: We considered word-skipping, first fixation durations, first run dwell time (sums of all fixation durations during first pass), go-past times, regressions to the target from later parts of the sentence, regressions from the target to earlier regions of the sentence.

issues.subcategory: unbalanced design with unmatched pre-target word counts
issues.description: The authors report that the number of words pre-target differed significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05). This is a significant confound for eye-tracking measures, as the amount of prior context affects sentence processing difficulty and integration demands. The authors note this difference but do not control for it in their analyses, potentially confounding the congruency effect with differences in sentence length and processing load prior to the target.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.subcategory: small and unequal sample sizes across experiments
issues.description: Experiments 1, 2, and 3 use 46, 29, and 47 participants respectively. Experiment 2 has only 29 participants, which is substantially smaller than the other experiments. No power analysis is reported for any experiment. Given that the key theoretical claims rest on graded effects of diagnosticity and specificity (continuous predictors), the power to detect these interaction effects—particularly in Experiment 2 with 29 participants—is likely inadequate. The unequal sample sizes also make cross-experiment comparisons difficult.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students... Participants were 29 undergraduate students... 47 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway University of London were recruited

issues.subcategory: lack of counterbalancing in Experiment 1
issues.description: In Experiment 1, stimuli were divided into two lists with 40 items per list, with each suffix occurring twice only. However, the assignment of specific nonwords to lists is not described as counterbalanced across participants. If the same nonwords always appear in the same list, any item-specific effects cannot be separated from list effects. Furthermore, with only two exposures per suffix, the reliability of suffix-level estimates used in the graded diagnosticity analyses is questionable.
issues.quote: stimuli were divided into two experimental lists with 40 items per list. Participants saw only one list; each suffix occurred twice only.

issues.subcategory: no item random effects in Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: The mixed models in Experiments 1 and 2 include only random intercepts for subjects, with no random effects for items (nonwords or suffixes). This means the analyses do not account for variability across items, violating the requirement for generalizability across both subjects and items (the 'language-as-fixed-effect fallacy'). Experiment 3 includes random intercepts for suffixes but not for individual nonword items. Without by-item random effects, the reported effects may not generalize beyond the specific stimuli used.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.subcategory: confound between morphological and orthographic cues in nonword design
issues.description: The authors explicitly state they did not include non-pseudoaffixed words 'because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).' However, this means the experiments cannot distinguish whether participants are responding to morphological knowledge (suffix meaning) or low-level orthographic regularities (letter patterns). The authors discuss this issue in the General Discussion but do not resolve it experimentally, weakening the core claim that morphological rather than orthographic regularities drive the effects.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).

issues.subcategory: potential demand characteristics from explicit category judgment task
issues.description: Experiment 1 requires participants to explicitly judge whether nonwords look like nouns or adjectives, and participants are told the definitions of these categories in the instructions. This explicit metalinguistic task may not reflect implicit knowledge of spelling-meaning regularities but rather conscious reasoning about word endings. The authors claim this tests 'explicit knowledge' but then use it as evidence alongside implicit measures (eye-tracking) to support the same theoretical conclusion, conflating explicit and implicit sensitivity.
issues.quote: Experiment 1 tested skilled readers' explicit knowledge of dependencies between spelling and lexical category... Participants were seated in a quiet room and read the following instructions: 'You will be asked to decide if a letter string looks like a noun or an adjective.'

issues.subcategory: uncontrolled phonological properties of nonwords across conditions
issues.description: In Experiment 3, the congruent and incongruent conditions use different nonwords (different stems combined with different suffixes). While the authors match pre- and post-target sentence regions on letter counts, they do not report matching of nonword properties such as length, phonological neighborhood size, or bigram frequency across congruent and incongruent conditions. Differences in these low-level properties could confound the congruency effect on eye-movement measures.
issues.quote: Eighty experimental nonwords with suffix spellings diagnostic for adjectives (10 suffixes) or nouns (10 suffixes) were selected from Experiment 1.

issues.subcategory: diagnosticity formula appears to describe relative frequency, not predictive validity
issues.description: The authors define type diagnosticity as 'the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category divided by the total number of words falling into this category.' This formula computes the proportion of all words in a category that end in a given suffix—essentially a measure of how common the suffix is among words of that category. This is not the same as how well the suffix predicts the category (which would be the proportion of words with the suffix that belong to the category). The authors acknowledge this resembles 'cue validity' but the formula as stated computes something closer to sensitivity/recall rather than precision/predictive value.
issues.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.subcategory: mismatch between predicted direction of diagnosticity and specificity effects
issues.description: The authors predict that diagnosticity (spelling-to-meaning) should influence tasks involving production of spelling, while specificity (meaning-to-spelling) should influence tasks involving reading/categorization. However, Experiment 1 (categorization from print) is analyzed using diagnosticity, and Experiment 2 (spelling production) uses specificity. This is the opposite of the stated theoretical prediction. The authors acknowledge this in the conclusion section but do not adequately explain why the mapping was reversed in the experimental design.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading).

issues.subcategory: lexical category operationalized as a proxy for 'meaning'
issues.description: The paper claims to investigate 'the relationship between spelling and meaning' but operationalizes meaning exclusively as lexical category (noun, adjective, verb). Lexical category is a syntactic/grammatical property, not a semantic one. The authors briefly acknowledge this ('This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category') but the abstract and title make broader claims about 'meaningful regularities' and 'meaningful information' that overstate what is actually being measured. The relationship between lexical category and meaning is theoretically contested.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of 'meaning').

issues.subcategory: comprehension accuracy reported as percentage rather than proportion
issues.description: The authors report 'Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86%' which, if taken literally, means participants answered correctly on less than 1% of trials—a nonsensical result. This is clearly a formatting error where the value should be 86% (or 0.86 as a proportion). However, the range reported (0.66% to 0.98%) is also inconsistent: if these are proportions (0.66 to 0.98), the mean of 0.86 is plausible, but the % sign is wrong throughout.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.subcategory: evolutionary/diachronic claims unsupported by presented data
issues.description: The authors make strong causal claims that English spelling 'evolved' and 'has become fractionated' to maximize meaningful information transmission, and that 'irregularity in the English spelling-sound mapping may permit regularity in the spelling-meaning mapping.' These are diachronic causal claims that cannot be supported by the synchronic corpus analysis and behavioral experiments presented. The diachronic evidence cited (Berg & Aronoff, 2017) is from a separate paper and is only briefly summarized, yet the authors treat it as supporting their causal evolutionary narrative.
issues.quote: English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information... it suggests that irregularity in the English spelling-sound mapping may permit regularity in the spelling-meaning mapping.

issues.subcategory: implicit statistical learning inferred without direct evidence
issues.description: The authors conclude that 'this knowledge was acquired through implicit statistical learning processes' based solely on the observation that participants were not explicitly taught the regularities. This is an inference by exclusion that does not constitute evidence for implicit statistical learning. Alternative explanations—such as explicit instruction in morphology during schooling, metalinguistic awareness developed through literacy education, or conscious analogical reasoning—are not ruled out. No measure of explicit vs. implicit knowledge was included.
issues.quote: It is unlikely that our participants were ever taught these relationships explicitly; more likely is that this knowledge was acquired through implicit statistical learning processes

issues.subcategory: direction of causality between spelling irregularity and meaning transmission unestablished
issues.description: The paper argues that spelling-sound inconsistency in English enables spelling-meaning regularity. However, the causal direction is not established: it is equally possible that spelling-meaning regularities arose for historical reasons unrelated to spelling-sound inconsistency, or that both properties are consequences of a third factor (e.g., borrowing from Latin/French). The computational analysis is purely correlational and cannot establish that one property caused or enabled the other.
issues.quote: the proliferation of spellings in English may actually be functional... the multiple spellings permissible for particular sound sequences seem to be fractionated in such a way as to allow particular spellings to become reserved for particular functions.

issues.subcategory: missing details on how suffix spellings were extracted from nonword responses in Experiment 2
issues.description: The authors state that 'suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings' but provide no details about inter-rater reliability, the criteria used for extraction, or how ambiguous cases were handled. Given that participants could spell nonwords in many ways, the extraction of the 'suffix portion' from a novel spelling requires judgment calls that could introduce systematic bias. Without reliability information, the validity of the dependent variable cannot be assessed.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings (1,914 analysable data points).

issues.subcategory: missing information about data exclusions and missing data in Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: Experiment 1 reports 1,625 data points with 11.7% missing due to timeouts or button press errors. With 46 participants and 40 items each, the expected total is 1,840 data points, meaning 215 are missing. No analysis of whether missing data is systematic (e.g., related to suffix type or participant characteristics) is provided. Experiment 2 reports 1,914 analysable data points but does not specify the total expected or the exclusion rate, nor whether exclusions were random.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.subcategory: model specification for Experiment 3 not fully reported
issues.description: For Experiment 3, the authors state 'All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes' and that 'in the interest of space we report only those effects pertaining to our main variable of interest.' The full model specifications (fixed effects, random effects structure, optimizer settings) are not provided in the paper, and readers are directed to OSF for the full report. Without the complete model specification, the reported results cannot be independently verified or replicated.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes. However, in the interest of space we report only those effects pertaining to our main variable of interest, congruency (congruent or incongruent). The full report can be found in the OSF storage for this project.

issues.subcategory: diagnosticity formula ambiguity regarding denominator
issues.description: The diagnosticity formula divides 'the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.' It is unclear whether 'total number of words falling into this category' refers to (a) all words in the CELEX database in that category, (b) all words containing any suffix in that category, or (c) all words containing this specific suffix in any category. The example given (–NIK has diagnosticity 0 for adjectives, –TUDE has diagnosticity 1 for nouns) is consistent with interpretation (c) but the formula text suggests (a). This ambiguity makes the measure impossible to replicate without clarification.
issues.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

issues.subcategory: no description of how congruent/incongruent sentence pairs were created or validated
issues.description: The paper describes sentence templates for noun, adjective, and verb contexts but provides no validation that these contexts reliably cued the intended lexical categories. No norming study or cloze probability data is reported to confirm that the sentence frames actually biased participants toward the intended category. Without such validation, it is unclear whether null effects (e.g., on first fixation duration) reflect genuine absence of early effects or inadequate context strength.
issues.quote: Sixty-six sentences were designed following one of three possible context templates (noun, adjective, or verb template; see Table 4 for an example of each template).

issues.subcategory: entropy analysis methodology underspecified
issues.description: The entropy analysis comparing Hspelling and Hsound is described briefly but key methodological details are missing: how many suffixes were included, whether the same 154 suffixes from the main analysis were used, how phonological forms were obtained for suffixes that have multiple pronunciations, and whether the regression was weighted by suffix frequency. The claim that 'spelling is more predictive of category compared to phonology' rests entirely on this analysis, yet it cannot be replicated from the information provided.
issues.quote: We calculated Hspelling to provide an estimate of the prediction precision from the suffix spelling, and we calculated Hsound to provide an estimate of the prediction precision from the most frequent pronunciation of the suffix. We then examined the slope of the regression equation lm(Hspelling ~ Hphonology).

issues.subcategory: WEIRD sample with no demographic reporting
issues.description: All three experiments use undergraduate students from a single UK university (Royal Holloway, University of London). No demographic information is reported (age, gender, reading ability, L1 background, years of education). The authors make broad claims about 'skilled readers' and 'literate adults' without acknowledging that their sample is restricted to young, highly educated, predominantly native English speakers at a single institution. The generalizability of findings to other populations (older adults, less educated readers, L2 speakers) is not discussed.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London... Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London... 47 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway University of London were recruited

issues.subcategory: overclaiming universality of diagnosticity and specificity across orthographies
issues.description: The authors claim that 'diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.' This is a strong universalist claim made without any cross-linguistic data. The authors acknowledge that 'further research is needed' but present this as a confident conjecture rather than a hypothesis, and the reasoning (that these reflect 'general cognitive principles') is circular and unsupported.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.subcategory: findings from nonwords generalized to real word reading
issues.description: All three experiments use nonwords as stimuli. The authors draw conclusions about how 'skilled readers' process real words and how 'English spelling may have become fractionated' to serve reading. However, nonword processing may engage different strategies than real word recognition (e.g., more reliance on sublexical rules, less top-down lexical knowledge). The generalization from nonword sensitivity to claims about the reading system's representation of real words is not empirically justified within this paper.
issues.quote: We have shown that literate adults are sensitive to these regularities between spelling and meaning, and that their long-term knowledge mirrors the strength of these regularities in the writing system.

issues.subcategory: misapplication of feedforward/feedback terminology
issues.description: The authors state they 'focus solely on what is usually referred to as feedforward effects' and define diagnosticity as influencing spelling production and specificity as influencing reading. However, in standard reading models, 'feedforward' refers to bottom-up processing from orthography to phonology/semantics, not to production. Using diagnosticity (a spelling-to-meaning measure) to predict spelling production is actually a feedback effect (meaning influencing spelling output), not feedforward. The theoretical framework is applied inconsistently.
issues.quote: we focus solely on what is usually referred to as 'feedforward' effects. That is, we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning

issues.subcategory: conflation of derivational and inflectional morphology
issues.description: The paper focuses on derivational suffixes but repeatedly uses inflectional examples (–ED for past tense) to motivate the theoretical framework. The computational analysis explicitly covers only derivational suffixes ('we extracted all spellings annotated as derivational suffixes in CELEX'), yet the introduction and discussion treat inflectional and derivational morphology interchangeably. The mechanisms underlying inflectional and derivational processing are theoretically distinct, and this conflation weakens the theoretical coherence of the paper.
issues.quote: Similar dependency characterizes English inflectional suffixes. For example, it is well known that spelling –ED is strongly indicative of past tense... Our analyses demonstrate definitively that the 154 English derivational suffixes studied are characterised by a high degree of diagnosticity and specificity

issues.subcategory: post-hoc sign transformation of diagnosticity variable
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the authors multiply diagnosticity by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes before entering it into the model. This transformation is described as a methodological choice to combine adjective and noun diagnosticity into a single predictor, but it is not pre-specified and introduces researcher degrees of freedom. The authors then conduct separate analyses for adjective and noun suffixes 'to make sure that this effect was not due to the sign-transformation,' suggesting awareness that the transformation could be problematic. The separate analyses show different patterns (adjective effect significant, noun effect marginal), which is not fully reconciled.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model... We performed this analysis separately for adjective- and noun- diagnostic suffixes to make sure that this effect was not due to the sign-transformation of the diagnosticity variable

issues.subcategory: selective reporting of token vs. type analyses
issues.description: The paper reports both type-based and token-based measures of diagnosticity and specificity, but the reporting of these analyses is inconsistent across experiments. In Experiment 1, token analyses show a weaker effect (adjective-specific suffixes show no effect of diagnosticity, p > 0.8). In Experiment 2, the token interaction z-value is reported as 0.60 (apparently non-significant despite the p < 0.01 claim). The authors note that 'token-based measures provided a poorer fit' but do not pre-specify which measure is primary, creating flexibility in which results to emphasize.
issues.quote: The results based on token measures were similar (main effect of diagnosticity, and an effect of diagnosticity on noun-diagnostic suffixes), but adjective-specific suffixes did not show an effect of diagnosticity (p > 0.8).

issues.subcategory: model comparison approach for interaction effects not pre-specified
issues.description: In Experiment 3, the authors test whether diagnosticity moderates congruency effects using model comparison (chi-square tests of model fit improvement). This approach is used selectively only for the two measures that showed significant main effects of congruency, not for all six measures. Applying model comparison only to significant outcomes constitutes a form of selective analysis that inflates Type I error. The decision to use model comparison rather than including the interaction in the primary model is not justified.
issues.quote: Further analyses investigated whether the size of the congruency effects on the go-past and regressions-out measures was influenced by the degree to which suffix spellings were diagnostic of lexical category. In order to assess this, we tested whether the addition of the interaction between diagnosticity and congruency would improve the fit of the models in these cases.

issues.subcategory: no analysis of whether trial exclusions in Experiment 3 are systematic
issues.description: Experiment 3 discards 4% of trials based on visual inspection of eye-tracking traces. No information is provided about whether these exclusions were distributed equally across congruent and incongruent conditions, or across suffix types. If incongruent trials (which are more difficult to process) are more likely to produce tracking artifacts or non-standard reading patterns, systematic exclusion of these trials would bias the results toward finding smaller congruency effects, potentially underestimating the true effect.
issues.quote: All trials were also visually inspected in order to identify those where participants had not read the sentences in full, or where any considerable deviation in the eye-tracking trace was evident during the trial. As a result of these checks, 4% of trials were discarded.

issues.subcategory: different numbers of analysable trials across eye-movement measures not explained
issues.description: The paper reports that regressions-in were available for 34% of trials and regressions-out for 15% of trials, but does not specify the total number of trials available for each measure or explain why these percentages differ so substantially. First fixation duration, first run dwell time, and go-past time require at least one fixation on the target, while regression measures require specific fixation patterns. The paper does not report how many trials were excluded from each analysis or whether exclusion rates differed by condition.
issues.quote: 34% of all trials available for analysis contained such regressions... 15% of all trials available for analysis contained such regressions.

issues.subcategory: missing information about viewing distance and visual angle calculations
issues.description: The paper reports a viewing distance of 140cm, which is unusually large for eye-tracking studies (typical distances are 50-80cm). At 140cm, the reported character width of 0.3 degrees corresponds to approximately 0.73mm per character, which seems implausibly small. The authors do not explain why such an unusual viewing distance was used, and the visual angle calculations should be verified. This detail is important for assessing whether the experimental setup was appropriate for detecting fixation differences on individual words.
issues.quote: Participants were seated at a viewing distance of 140cm, with this position maintained with a table-mounted head and chin rest... black Courier font (size 14pt, horizontal character width 0.3o)

issues.subcategory: contradictory description of +ally suffix
issues.description: Appendix A lists +ally with diagnosticity values of 0 for all three categories (A=0, N=0, V=0) and specificity values of NA for all categories, with a type frequency of 397. A suffix with 397 tokens but zero diagnosticity for any category is theoretically impossible if the suffix occurs in real words—every word must belong to some lexical category. This likely reflects a classification issue (adverbs are not included as a category), but the zero values without explanation are misleading and suggest the analysis has a systematic gap in its category coverage.

issues.subcategory: adverb category systematically excluded without justification
issues.description: The computational analysis considers only three lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs. Adverbs are a major lexical category in English and many derivational suffixes (notably –LY, –ALLY, –WARD, –WARDS, –WISE) primarily or exclusively form adverbs. The exclusion of adverbs means that suffixes like –LY (the most frequent suffix in the database with 2717 tokens) receive diagnosticity values of near-zero for all three included categories, severely distorting the analysis. The authors do not justify this exclusion or discuss its implications for their conclusions about the English derivational system.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs... +ly | 0.039 | 0.006 | 0.002 | 1.000 | 1.000 | NA | 2717
issues.location: computational analysis methods and Appendix A
